quizTarget: A source paragraph starts, then a section starts before that paragraph is closed. Does indenting the section farther right make it a paragraph child?
reasoning: Content rules, not indentation or id, determine how this malformed paragraph is recovered.

essentialSupport.fact: The source is the text you write. The DOM (Document Object Model) is the tree of elements the browser builds from that text. They can differ when the source breaks a nesting rule. A tolerant parser can recover a page without making the original source conforming HTML.

A p holds phrasing content, such as text and emphasis. A section is not phrasing content. Starting section while a paragraph is open makes the HTML parser close that paragraph first. Indentation does not override this rule.

This deliberately malformed fragment belongs in a disposable body for inspection, not in your finished page. ```html

Start

Details
Finish

``` The section becomes a sibling of the paragraph, not its child. Finish is outside the original paragraph. The unmatched closing p can also produce an empty paragraph. The DOM inspector shows the recovered tree; View Source still shows what was written.

Write separate, properly closed siblings instead. A validator checks authoring rules; a DOM inspector shows the resulting tree. Neither tool judges whether the prose is useful. For this task keep Start and Finish in their own paragraphs around the Details section. No particular browser DevTools interface is required to answer the check.

quizTarget: You add a second dd immediately after the description for Return, without inserting another dt. Which name does the new description belong to?
reasoning: The consecutive descriptions remain in the Return group until a new name group starts.

essentialSupport.fact: A description list associates names with descriptions. dl wraps the list, dt supplies a name, and dd supplies its description. Use it for a small glossary or a set of labeled facts, not merely to indent text.

Within the simple pattern here, one dt followed by two dd elements gives two descriptions for that name. A new dt starts the next group. These are not numbered steps; use ol when sequence is the point.

Put this fragment inside body.

```html
<dl><dt>Collection point</dt><dd>East desk</dd><dt>Return time</dt><dd>Before closing</dd></dl>
```

East desk describes Collection point. Before closing describes Return time. The next dt changes which name the following description belongs to.

Give Pickup the description Blue shelf, then give Return both descriptions Friday and Before 4 pm. Keep both return descriptions before any next dt. The checks inspect association through order; they cannot tell whether the real desk accepts returns then.

quizTarget: You add cite="https://example.org/journal" to blockquote but add no visible source text. Does that attribute itself display an attribution line?
reasoning: The cite attribute stores a source address; it is not ordinary rendered attribution text.

essentialSupport.fact: blockquote marks a quoted block; q marks a short quotation within a sentence. Markup describes that relationship, not whether the quotation is accurate or legally reusable. The words in this lesson were invented for this exercise, not taken from a publication.

The cite attribute can store a source URL. Browsers do not ordinarily turn that attribute into a visible source label. A cite element, which is different from the attribute, marks the title of a work. Put readable attribution in ordinary page content when readers need it.

This fragment shows a block quotation and a separate source description. ```html

Leave the path clearer than you found it.

From Trail volunteer notes, an invented example.

``` The URL is metadata on blockquote. Trail volunteer notes remains visible inside cite. Merely changing the URL would not rewrite those visible words. For a short inline quote, use a q element in a sentence, for example

The invented note says Leave a clear path.

. A browser normally supplies quotation punctuation for q; do not add a second pair merely to imitate its default appearance.

Mark the invented notebook statement as a block quotation. Store its source URL and display Notebook practice as the work title outside the quote. A parser can verify these separate roles, not the truth or permission status of a real quotation.

quizTarget: A time element stores datetime="2026-12-03". You change only its text to 4 December. Has its stored date changed?
reasoning: Attribute and content are separate. Update both deliberately so they do not conflict.

essentialSupport.fact: time marks a date, time or duration. For this lesson use a calendar date. Its datetime attribute supplies a machine-readable value, while the text inside supplies the words readers see.

A calendar date here uses four-digit year, two-digit month and two-digit day, separated by hyphens: YYYY-MM-DD. This is not a promise that any arbitrary date-like string is valid. The actual month and day must also form a valid date.

Place this fragment in body. ```html

Next meeting: 8 November.

``` A reader sees 8 November. The attribute also provides the year, 2026. Changing only the visible text leaves datetime unchanged, which can create conflicting information.

Write a collection date of 3 December 2026. Use exactly Thursday, 3 December as the visible wording and the matching normalized attribute. These checks compare the two supplied representations; the lesson does not parse locale-dependent dates or create calendar appointments.

quizTarget: A street location is merely the meeting venue, not contact information for the page or an article. Must it use address?
reasoning: address has a contact-information role, not a rule that all postal locations belong inside it.

essentialSupport.fact: abbr marks an abbreviation. If supplied, title gives its full expansion, but a hover tooltip is not a reliable way for everyone to get that information. Explain an unfamiliar abbreviation in visible text the first time it matters.

address marks contact information for its nearest article or the document body. It is not a generic wrapper for every street address. A venue location in an ordinary paragraph need not use address. mailto: links ask the device to open an email handler; they do not send mail by themselves.

Both fragments can be placed in body. ```html

Estimated time of arrival (ETA) is noon.

Questions about this page: Page editor
``` The expansion is visible before ETA, even if title is not exposed by a device. The address block identifies the person responsible for this page, not the event venue.

Expand Community repair day visibly before CRD and supply its expansion as title. Add a separate address for the page contact. No email is sent by this exercise, and a matching mailto address is not proof the mailbox exists.

quizTarget: Inside pre, you remove the two spaces before the second line but keep its newline. What changes?
reasoning: pre preserves meaningful whitespace; removing the spaces changes the content layout, not whether code runs.

essentialSupport.fact: pre marks preformatted text: spaces and line breaks matter. code marks computer code. They have different jobs, so pre can wrap code when both apply. Ordinary paragraphs normally collapse runs of spaces for display.

pre does not turn HTML parsing off. Use already-learned character references for angle brackets that should be text. Keep a wanted first character immediately after the opening tag: HTML treats a newline immediately after a pre start tag specially by ignoring that first newline.

This example contains a real line break and two spaces before second. ```html 
first
  second
``` The text content is first, a newline, two spaces, then second. pre preserves that layout purpose; code supplies code semantics. Neither element executes the text.

Write open, then a newline and two spaces before save, then a newline and close. Do not use repeated br elements to simulate the stored code text. The task tests exact text content, not font or screen dimensions.

quizTarget: An image shows two different leaf outlines, while its caption says where they were observed. Can you remove alt merely because the caption exists?
reasoning: Caption and alt can convey different facts. Preserve an appropriate replacement for the informative image.

essentialSupport.fact: figure groups content that can be treated as one unit, such as an illustration with its caption. figcaption supplies the caption and belongs first or last inside figure. A figure need not be an image, but this lesson uses one.

A caption can explain context or significance. alt supplies the useful information lost if the image cannot be seen. Do not assume a caption makes alt unnecessary, and avoid needlessly repeating identical wording in both.

This fragment references an independently drawn diagram, not a borrowed photograph. Save the matching asset beside the page to view it locally. ```html ``` The alt text names the three shapes. The caption says where the observation came from. These are different useful facts. Merely writing src does not create the image file.

Group the leaf diagram and its caption. Keep the two outline shapes in the image description and the observation context in the caption. Automatic checks can inspect text and grouping, not establish whether the picture truly matches its description.

quizTarget: A search service shows different wording from your meta description. Does that alone mean your HTML description failed to parse?
reasoning: The description supplies metadata, not a command that every external service must display verbatim.

essentialSupport.fact: A meta element with name="description" gives a short description of the document through content. It is not an ordinary visible paragraph. Search services may use it, replace it or ignore it; writing it does not guarantee a particular search snippet or ranking.

A link with rel="icon" names an icon resource. href gives its location, while type can state its media type. The file must exist, and each browser chooses how and where to display it. This differs from an a link with clickable words in the body.

These fragments belong inside head, beside the existing title and charset metadata.

```html
<meta name="description" content="Short observations from a neighborhood tree survey.">
<link rel="icon" href="tree-mark.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
```

The description is stored in content. The icon link points to tree-mark.svg; it does not contain the picture. Use your own asset or one whose license permits your use, retaining required notices.

Give Cloud notebook the supplied short description and a link to cloud-mark.svg. Keep its title and visible h1 separate. The exercise checks metadata structure; it does not contact search engines or prove icon rendering. The companion icon is original markup supplied with this lesson.

quizTarget: You add download="saved.txt" to a link on another origin. Does that guarantee the browser saves the remote response using that name?
reasoning: download expresses a requested behavior and optional filename; it is not a universal override or proof that a download happened.

essentialSupport.fact: target="_blank" asks for a new browsing context, commonly a tab or window. The browser and user settings decide its presentation. Tell readers when a link intentionally opens a new context rather than making the change a surprise.

rel="noopener" prevents the opened context from receiving the ordinary opener relationship; modern _blank links already have this protection by default, but spelling it out makes the intention clear. download suggests saving a resource and can suggest a filename. It is not a command that overrides cross-origin rules, server headers or browser decisions.

Place these anchors in body. The guide URL is only an example destination; no external page is fetched during checks. ```html Open the guide in a new tab or window Download the checklist ``` The first link asks for a new context. The second points to a same-origin/local text resource and suggests trip-checklist.txt as its saved name. That file must actually exist. Neither attribute means a network operation has succeeded.

Make the map link explicitly request a new context and opener isolation. Make the notes link suggest field-notes.txt as its download name. The supplied checks inspect attributes only; test actual navigation/download separately in a suitable browser with real files.

quizTarget: You set lang="fr" on only the greeting span inside an English main. What happens to the surrounding English text?
reasoning: A descendant language attribute overrides its own subtree, not its ancestors or neighboring content.

essentialSupport.fact: lang identifies the language of an element and its descendants unless a descendant overrides it. A short passage in another language can carry its own lang. This helps tools interpret the content; it does not translate the words.

dir controls text direction: ltr, rtl or auto. It is not a language code. bdi isolates a piece of bidirectional text so its direction does not unintentionally affect surrounding text. dir="auto" lets direction be determined from that isolated text, useful for names supplied by different people.

These are ordinary text fragments, not generated translations. ```html

A visitor wrote hola.

Contributor: نور — 3 notes

``` The main region supplies English as the default. Only hola is marked Spanish. The name is isolated beside the count; neither lang nor bdi changes the stored characters. Actual visual ordering should be reviewed in a browser, not inferred from textContent alone.

Keep the main region English, mark bonjour as French and isolate the author name with automatic direction. Structural checks confirm the markup contract, not screen-reader pronunciation or the exact visual ordering in every font.

quizTarget: Only the main id changes from reading to observations. Does the unchanged skip link still identify that main?
reasoning: The fragment and id must agree. A main landmark and focus setting do not repair a mismatched address.

essentialSupport.fact: A skip link lets someone bypass repeated navigation and reach the main content. Keep this example’s link visible and first in the interactive reading order. A landmark and a fragment link are prior ideas; the new goal is a usable bypass route.

href="#reading" names a fragment; main id="reading" supplies its unique destination. tabindex="-1" lets the target receive focus without adding it to the ordinary Tab sequence. This is useful for a main-content target, not a reason to remove an ordinary action button from keyboard navigation. Never use a positive tabindex here to rearrange the reading order.

```html Skip to reading
HomeNotes

River observations

Today the water is clear.

Next observation
``` The first link targets main rather than the navigation itself. In a real browser, Tab to the skip link, activate it with Enter, then inspect where focus and the next Tab move. Merely scrolling to the heading is not the complete focus check. Keep a visible focus indicator; do not hide the outline.

Build the shown visible Skip to reading link before a named nav. Supply one main with id reading, tabindex -1, a heading and a later link. The referenced navigation files would need to exist to test those separate destinations. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Basil changes from th scope="row" to ordinary td. What changed?
reasoning: A cell’s text and header semantics are separate. tfoot and table markup do not perform arithmetic.

essentialSupport.fact: A data value can need two labels: its row and its column. Earlier tables mentioned scope="row"; now use it in a complete table, alongside column headers and a total row.

th marks a header cell. scope="row" associates it with its row; scope="col" associates it with its column. tbody groups ordinary data rows. tfoot groups a footer such as a total; it does not calculate that total. caption names the table as a whole, not each number.

```html
Seed packets packed
VarietyPackets
Basil4
Dill6
Total10
``` The value 4 belongs to the Basil row and Packets column. The footer’s 10 is authored text, not a formula. Replacing Basil’s th with td would leave visible text but remove that explicit header-cell relationship. Screen-reader announcement details still need real assistive-technology testing.

Build the packet table with two column headers, Basil and Dill row headers, and a Total row in tfoot. Keep the caption and the stated values. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: The 8 cell’s headers changes to "studio season june", but the cell stays visually under May. Is its explicit month relationship still correct?
reasoning: The headers tokens identify header elements. Valid IDs can still express the wrong relationship; existence checks alone cannot judge meaning.

essentialSupport.fact: A spanning cell covers several grid positions. It does not, by that fact alone, explain every data cell’s headers. For this small two-level table, explicitly name each relevant header rather than relying on visual alignment.

colspan="2" makes Spring occupy two columns; rowspan="2" makes Room occupy two header rows. A th id names one header uniquely. A td headers attribute is a space-separated list of those header IDs: not visible labels and not CSS selectors. This example uses explicit headers relationships rather than mixing in an unexplained scope="colgroup" strategy.

```html
Workshop bookings
RoomSpring
MayJune
Studio85
``` The 8 cell names Studio, Spring and May through studio season may. The 5 cell names Studio, Spring and June. The May and June cells occupy the two positions beneath Spring; Room already occupies the first position in both header rows. Keep tables as simple as the data permits, and test complex relationships with assistive technology.

Build this three-column bookings table. Keep the two spans, unique header IDs and explicit headers lists on both data cells. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Remove checked from early and leave both radios required. What is initially selected?
reasoning: required constrains acceptable submission; it is not a default-value setter. The shared name still prevents two simultaneous selections.

essentialSupport.fact: A radio group offers mutually exclusive choices. Sharing a name within the same form permits at most one selected radio; it does not force an initial selection. required adds the validation requirement that the group have a selection.

type="radio" chooses the control kind. Both inputs use name="slot" to form one group, but unique ids connect their own labels. value chooses the submitted value, not the visible label. checked supplies a default selection. required on a member makes the same-name group required; repeating it on both here keeps that intention clear. fieldset and legend name the overall question.

```html
<form id="visit">
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Choose a visit time</legend>
    <input type="radio" id="early" name="slot" value="early" required checked><label for="early">Early visit</label>
    <input type="radio" id="late" name="slot" value="late" required><label for="late">Late visit</label>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Request time</button>
</form>
```
Initially the selected early input contributes slot=early. The unchecked late input contributes nothing. Choosing late in a real browser deselects early and changes the submitted pair. Without either checked attribute the page may start with no selection; required does not automatically choose one. Native validation is separate from simply constructing form data.

Build the two required choices with unique labels and the Early visit default. Keep both name attributes equal to slot. The local data check reads the default; manually test keyboard radio movement and a required empty group in a real browser. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Change only rows from 4 to 8. Has the maxlength limit doubled?
reasoning: rows and maxlength have separate jobs. Neither changing height nor retaining default text rewrites the length attribute.

essentialSupport.fact: textarea provides a multiline text control. Unlike an input’s value attribute, its initial text goes between opening and closing tags. A label remains necessary; existing text is not a substitute for the field name.

rows="4" requests a visible height measured in text lines, not a four-line submission limit. maxlength="80" sets a text-length limit measured in UTF-16 code units; one visible character can occupy more than one unit. name="note" supplies the submitted key. This example is optional because required is absent.

```html
<form>
  <label for="note">Observation</label>
  <textarea id="note" name="note" rows="4" maxlength="80">Saw two moths.</textarea>
  <button type="submit">Send observation</button>
</form>
```
The initial field text is Saw two moths. A value="Other text" attribute on textarea would not supply its initial value. Users can edit the content; the original text in markup is the default, not a live copy of later edits. Browser user-entry limits and scripted changes have different constraint-validation rules, so do not infer typing behavior from an attribute check.

Create the labeled note textarea with four visible rows, an eighty-unit limit and the supplied initial text between its tags. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Change step to 1, keeping min=0 and value=0.5. Is 0.5 on the permitted step grid?
reasoning: With an explicit min of zero, the grid is 0,1,2. Range and step are independent constraints; the initial value need not be valid.

essentialSupport.fact: A numeric field can constrain both a range and a step grid. Being between the endpoints is not enough when a value falls between permitted steps. These browser constraints help users; the receiving server must still validate all data.

type="number" selects numeric entry. min="0" and max="2" include their endpoints. step="0.25" permits quarter-unit increments from the step base; here min sets that base to zero. Without a min, the value attribute can set the base, otherwise zero is used for this type. The default step is 1 if omitted; step="any" removes the step-grid restriction, not min/max. required rejects blank entry during ordinary validated submission.

```html

Enter 0 to 2 grams in quarter-gram steps.

``` The initial 0.5 is on the quarter-unit grid. 0.6 is within the range but off that grid. Zero is a numeric value and differs from an empty field. The optional JavaScript property valueAsNumber belongs to a later scripting bridge; this markup lesson does not teach or test numeric conversion code. Browser spin buttons and error messages can vary.

Build the mass field with the shown bounds, quarter-unit step, initial 0.5 and visible connected instructions. In a local browser, try blank, zero, 0.6 and 2; distinguish missing, step mismatch and acceptable boundary cases. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Replace readonly with disabled on reference. What happens to reference in ordinary form data?
reasoning: A name alone is insufficient for a disabled control to participate. readonly and disabled have different submission behavior.

essentialSupport.fact: A text field can be noneditable yet still participate in form data. readonly and disabled are different states. Earlier work established disabled omission; here compare that omission with a readonly field and a hidden value.

readonly on a supported text input prevents ordinary user editing while leaving it normally focusable and submitted when named. disabled prevents ordinary interaction and excludes this input from form data. Both are Boolean attributes. readonly does not apply to every control type, such as select or checkbox. A hidden input has no ordinary visible control but can still submit its name/value.

```html
<form id="booking">
  <label for="reference">Booking reference</label><input id="reference" name="reference" value="R17" readonly>
  <label for="estimate">Draft estimate</label><input id="estimate" name="estimate" value="12" disabled>
  <input type="hidden" name="revision" value="2">
  <button type="submit">Confirm</button>
</form>
```
The local data contains reference=R17 and revision=2, but not estimate. Constructing FormData in the supplied checker reads these pairs without contacting a server. Hidden and readonly values are not trusted secrets: a person can inspect or change page data outside normal editing, so the server must verify them independently.

Build the labeled readonly reference, labeled disabled estimate and hidden revision exactly as shown. Keep the two visible labels even though neither field is ordinarily editable. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Remove selected from Poppy, leaving all option text and values unchanged. What are the initial seed values?
reasoning: Form data uses selected options. Group labels organize choices but do not become selected values.

essentialSupport.fact: One submitted name can have several values. A multiple select preserves each selected option as a separate name/value pair; it does not automatically join those values into one comma-separated string.

multiple permits multiple selections. size="4" requests four visible rows, not a four-choice limit. optgroup label names a group of options; it is not itself a selectable answer. option value is the data value, while its text is the visible choice. selected sets an initial selection. Without required, selecting nothing is allowed.

```html
<form id="seeds">
  <label for="choices">Seeds to request</label>
  <select id="choices" name="seed" multiple size="4">
    <optgroup label="Herbs"><option value="basil" selected>Basil</option><option value="dill">Dill</option></optgroup>
    <optgroup label="Flowers"><option value="poppy" selected>Poppy</option></optgroup>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Request seeds</button>
</form>
```
Initially this form contributes seed=basil and seed=poppy, in document order. The supplied checker uses FormData.getAll("seed") to inspect all local values; that is test infrastructure, not an HTML function to implement. A single-value lookup would not represent the whole collection. Browser keyboard/touch selection gestures vary, so instructions should not promise one universal modifier key.

Build the two named option groups with Basil and Poppy initially selected. Use name seed for the select, not a different name on each option. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Change accept to image/png. Does that prove every file reaching the server is a valid PNG?
reasoning: accept guides selection, and multipart packages data. Neither verifies actual file contents or prevents altered requests.

essentialSupport.fact: A file input lets a person choose local files deliberately. Selecting a file is not the same as uploading it. This exercise configures the markup only: it does not choose real personal files or contact an upload service.

type="file" requests a file chooser. multiple permits more than one chosen file. accept="image/png,image/jpeg" suggests image types to the chooser; it is not a trustworthy validation rule. name="photos" supplies the form field name. For a form sending files, method="post" with enctype="multipart/form-data" configures multipart encoding. action names a receiving route, which must actually be implemented.

```html

Choose PNG or JPEG photos you intend to share. Selection alone does not upload them.

``` There is no value containing a local path. A page cannot prefill an arbitrary local file selection by writing a path into the markup. Browsers may display a privacy-preserving fake path rather than a real filesystem location. A real receiving server must check size, content and authorization; filenames or accept hints are not sufficient. Do not activate Send on this example expecting a working service.

Build the optional labeled photos control, type hints, multiple selection and multipart POST configuration. Keep the visible explanation. Checks inspect attributes, not picker UI, file decoding or upload success. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: Remove only form="draft" from the outside Preview button. Does its name/value still associate it with that form?
reasoning: The form attribute references a form ID. name contributes data only when a button is an associated submitter; it does not establish ownership.

essentialSupport.fact: A form may have several submit buttons with different intentions. The particular button that initiates submission is the submitter. Its own name/value can join the form data; other submit buttons are not all included merely because they exist.

type="submit" chooses a submission button. name="intent" and value="save" or "preview" describe its contributed pair. form="draft" associates the outside Preview button with the form whose id is draft. formaction and formmethod on that submit button override the form’s action and method for that submission only. They do not rewrite the form element.

```html
<form id="draft" action="/save" method="post">
  <label for="title">Draft title</label><input id="title" name="title" value="Pond notes">
  <button id="save" type="submit" name="intent" value="save">Save draft</button>
</form>
<button id="preview" type="submit" form="draft" name="intent" value="preview" formaction="/preview" formmethod="get">Preview draft</button>
```
Activating Save requests POST /save with title and intent=save. Activating Preview requests GET /preview with title and intent=preview. GET exposes data in the URL query, so use only the fictional nonsensitive title here. The endpoints are not implemented. Constructing FormData(form) without a submitter does not simulate clicking a particular button; the exercise checks association and attributes without navigation.

Build the draft form with its labeled title and Save button. Put the Preview button outside it, associate it using form=draft, and give it the stated GET preview overrides. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.

quizTarget: With type="text" but inputmode="email", what supplies email syntax validation?
reasoning: The changed control remains a text input. A keyboard suggestion and a data-purpose hint do not impose the email type constraint.

essentialSupport.fact: Prerequisite: labeled inputs. autocomplete tells the browser what personal-data field this is. The email token identifies an email address; it is not the name used to submit the field.

inputmode="email" suggests an email-friendly keyboard. type="email" supplies email syntax constraints; autocomplete and inputmode do not. Browser settings and context can prevent autofill. Never assume a suggested keyboard prevents other text.

```html
<form>
<label for="contact">Contact email</label>
<input id="contact" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" inputmode="email">
</form>
```

```html
<form>
<label for="contact">Contact email</label>
<input id="contact" name="email" type="text" autocomplete="email" inputmode="email">
</form>
```
The changed control remains a text input. A keyboard suggestion and a data-purpose hint do not impose the email type constraint.
Optional: change one relevant value, predict the effect, and compare the parsed attributes. Structural checks do not prove browser presentation or accessibility.

quizTarget: If only aria-invalid changes to false while value stays ab12, does the pattern become satisfied?
reasoning: ARIA communicates an error state; the pattern still examines the actual value. Change both the value and the feedback when correction succeeds.

essentialSupport.fact: Prerequisite: required fields and connected help. pattern constrains the entire nonempty value of a supported text input. Here [A-Z] means one uppercase ASCII letter, [0-9] one digit, and {2} repeats the preceding set twice. required separately rejects blank input.

aria-invalid="true" communicates a known error; it does not create or clear native validity. aria-describedby lists IDs of help/error text. This is a static invalid-state snapshot, not an automatic error updater. A real form must update the message and state after correction and revalidate on the server.

```html

Use two uppercase letters followed by two digits, such as AB12.

The entered code has lowercase letters. Change them to uppercase.

```

```html

The code format is now valid.

``` ARIA communicates an error state; the pattern still examines the actual value. Change both the value and the feedback when correction succeeds.

quizTarget: Does changing lazy to eager remove the supplied aspect ratio?
reasoning: Loading policy and dimension hints are independent attributes. The changed example retains the same dimensions.

essentialSupport.fact: Prerequisite: image source and alternative text. Numeric width and height attributes describe dimensions in CSS pixels and provide an aspect-ratio hint before an image finishes loading. The original asset here is 640 by 320, a 2:1 ratio.

loading="lazy" allows deferred loading for an image away from the initial view. eager is the normal immediate-loading behavior. Do not routinely lazy-load the prominent first image. These hints do not guarantee request timing or measure layout stability; CSS can still alter final dimensions.

quizTarget: At a 500 CSS-pixel viewport, what slot width does the changed sizes hint describe?
reasoning: Use the matching media condition first, then compute its vw fraction of the viewport. At 800 pixels the condition fails and the final 320px hint applies. The candidate selection remains the browser’s decision.

quizTarget: If defer is replaced by async, can the script assume the later paragraph already exists?
reasoning: async does not guarantee the parsed-DOM or ordering contract supplied by defer.

essentialSupport.fact: An external classic script with defer downloads without blocking parsing and runs after parsing, before DOMContentLoaded. Deferred classic scripts preserve document order. An external async script executes when ready and does not promise that order or a completed document. defer has no effect on an inline classic script.

type="module" selects JavaScript module semantics and normally defers execution; async on a module requests execution as soon as its graph is ready. Modules introduce fetch/CORS and dependency rules, not merely a renamed classic script. This app strips scripts from HTML submissions, so this unit is concept-only. Never interpret a stripped preview as a scheduling test.
```html
<script async src="stage.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="module-stage.js"></script>
```
These are alternative declarations, not extra tags to add to the companion. The module file is deliberately not supplied: this reference illustrates the loading contract rather than claiming a tested module application.

Save these two files beside each other. index.html: ```html Deferred script study

Inputs are the ID and new string; the effect is an updated paragraph, not an HTML insertion. Open the local index.html in a browser to inspect this classic-script example. This manual companion has not been verified merely by reading these files.

quizTarget: With popover="manual", should clicking outside be assumed to dismiss it automatically?
reasoning: The manual state changes dismissal behavior. The trigger still references the same panel, and no modal contract has been created.

essentialSupport.fact: Prerequisites: disclosure and dialog distinction. popover="auto" declares a nonmodal overlay. A button’s popovertarget points to its unique ID and, by default, toggles it. In a supporting browser, auto popovers support light dismissal such as clicking outside. They do not make the rest of the document inert like a modal dialog.

popover="manual" omits automatic light dismissal. Neither declaration alone proves browser support. This app checks the attributes only; JSDOM is not evidence of native top-layer behavior, focus handling, Escape, or dismissal. In a browser, the supplied expression "popover" in HTMLElement.prototype tests API presence, not accessibility quality. Unsupported hosts need an appropriate readable fallback.

quizTarget: After removing only progress value, what does that progress element mean?
reasoning: No value means indeterminate progress. It does not assert that zero of eight chapters have been reviewed. The changed snapshot deliberately retains stale fallback text (3 of 8); a real UI must also update that text to an honest unknown-progress message.

essentialSupport.fact: Prerequisite: explicit labels. progress represents task completion: value is work completed and max is the positive total. Omitting value means indeterminate progress, not zero completion. meter instead describes a scalar measurement within a known range, such as percentage of storage used.

For meter, min/max bound the range, low/high divide it into regions, and optimum identifies a preferred value. Here 10 is in the low region, while 90 is above high=80: greater storage use is less desirable. Styling and color are browser-dependent; keep meaningful labels and text rather than relying on color.

```html
<label for="done">Chapters reviewed</label>
<progress id="done" value="3" max="8">3 of 8</progress>
<label for="space">Notebook space used</label>
<meter id="space" min="0" max="100" low="20" high="80" optimum="10" value="90">90 percent</meter>
```
